learningObjectives.title: Charles I's Personal Rule and the causes of the Civil War
The English Civil War and the execution of Charles I
The Interregnum, Cromwell and the Restoration of 1660

questions.q: In which year did Charles I begin his period of 'Personal Rule', governing without calling Parliament?
questions.explain: Charles dissolved Parliament in 1629 and did not call another for eleven years, a period known as the Personal Rule.

questions.q: Which unpopular tax, traditionally levied only on coastal areas, did Charles I extend to inland counties during the Personal Rule?
questions.explain: Charles controversially extended Ship Money to inland counties to raise revenue without Parliament.

questions.q: Who was the Archbishop of Canterbury whose religious reforms angered many Puritans during the Personal Rule?
questions.explain: Archbishop William Laud's High Church reforms were seen by Puritans as moving dangerously close to Catholicism.

questions.q: Why did Charles I's attempt to impose a new Prayer Book on Scotland in 1637 contribute to the outbreak of war?
options: It provoked Scottish rebellion, forcing Charles to recall Parliament to fund the Bishops' Wars
It caused the immediate execution of Archbishop Laud
It led the Scots to invade Ireland
It persuaded Parliament to grant Charles more money
questions.explain: Scottish resistance triggered the Bishops' Wars, and needing money to fight them forced Charles to end the Personal Rule.

questions.q: Which of Charles I's chief ministers, known for his policy of 'Thorough', was executed in 1641?
questions.explain: Thomas Wentworth, Earl of Strafford, was executed by Act of Attainder in 1641 after pressure from Parliament.

questions.q: The Grand Remonstrance of 1641 is best described as which of the following?
options: A long list of Parliament's grievances against Charles I's rule
A peace treaty ending the Civil War
A tax imposed on the gentry
A declaration of war by the Scots
questions.explain: The Grand Remonstrance set out Parliament's complaints against Charles and deepened the divide between king and Parliament.

questions.q: In January 1642 Charles I entered the House of Commons with soldiers to arrest five MPs but found them gone. What does this event most clearly suggest?
options: That Charles had lost trust in Parliament and was willing to use force, worsening the crisis
That Parliament fully supported the king
That the Civil War had already ended
That the MPs had fled abroad permanently
questions.explain: The failed arrest of the Five Members shattered remaining trust and pushed both sides towards armed conflict.

questions.q: In which year did Charles I raise his standard at Nottingham, marking the start of the First Civil War?
questions.explain: Charles raised his royal standard at Nottingham in August 1642, signalling the beginning of the Civil War.

questions.q: By what name were the supporters of Parliament in the Civil War commonly known?
questions.explain: Parliament's supporters were nicknamed Roundheads, while the Royalists were called Cavaliers.

questions.q: Which 1645 battle was the decisive Parliamentarian victory that effectively broke the Royalist cause?
questions.explain: The Battle of Naseby in 1645 was a crushing defeat for the Royalists and effectively decided the First Civil War.

questions.q: Why was the creation of the New Model Army in 1645 significant for Parliament's war effort?
options: It was a professional, well-disciplined national army promoted on merit rather than status
It was made up entirely of Scottish soldiers
It fought only for the king
It refused to accept any Puritan soldiers
questions.explain: The New Model Army was a full-time, professionally trained force whose discipline and merit-based promotion gave Parliament a decisive advantage.

questions.q: Who was the commander-in-chief of the New Model Army when it was formed in 1645?
questions.explain: Sir Thomas Fairfax was appointed commander-in-chief of the New Model Army, with Cromwell leading its cavalry.

questions.q: What was 'Pride's Purge' of December 1648?
options: The forcible removal of MPs likely to oppose putting the king on trial
A tax raised to pay the New Model Army
The abolition of the House of Lords
questions.explain: Colonel Pride's soldiers excluded MPs opposed to trying the king, leaving the 'Rump' Parliament that agreed to Charles's trial.

questions.q: On what date was Charles I executed outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall?
questions.explain: Charles I was beheaded on 30 January 1649, the only English monarch to be executed by his own subjects.

questions.q: A source describes Charles I at his trial refusing to recognise the court's authority. Which idea does this best reflect?
options: His belief in the Divine Right of Kings, that he answered only to God
His acceptance that Parliament could judge a king
His wish to abdicate the throne
questions.explain: Charles argued that no earthly court could try a king, reflecting his firm belief in the Divine Right of Kings.

questions.q: What was the name given to the republic established in England after the execution of Charles I?
questions.explain: England was declared a Commonwealth, a republic without a monarch or House of Lords, in 1649.

questions.q: What title did Oliver Cromwell take when he became head of state in December 1653?
questions.explain: Under the Instrument of Government, Cromwell became Lord Protector, ruling for the rest of his life.

questions.q: Why did the 'Rule of the Major-Generals' (1655-1657) make Cromwell's government unpopular?
options: It imposed strict military and moral control over the regions, resented as harsh and intrusive
It restored the monarchy against people's wishes
It gave power back to the Catholic Church
questions.explain: Dividing England into districts under army officers who enforced Puritan rules was widely resented as oppressive military rule.

questions.q: Following Cromwell's death in 1658, why did the republic collapse and lead towards the Restoration?
options: His son Richard proved a weak ruler, and the army and Parliament fell into disorder
Charles II was already ruling in London
The New Model Army was disbanded by the Scots
questions.explain: Richard Cromwell lacked authority over the army, and the resulting instability paved the way for the monarchy's return.

questions.q: In 1660 General George Monck marched his army from Scotland to London and helped arrange free elections. What was the main outcome of his actions?
options: The recall of Charles II and the Restoration of the monarchy
A new civil war between England and Scotland
questions.explain: Monck's intervention led to a new Parliament that invited Charles II to return, restoring the monarchy in 1660.
